scenes.title: Too many points
lines: This is a map of four made-up counties.
Their outlines use about eleven hundred points, far more than it takes to draw the map this small.
Simplification throws points away, so the map is smaller to send and faster to draw.
The question is what else gets thrown away with them.

scenes.title: How Douglas–Peucker works
lines: The usual method is Douglas–Peucker.
Draw a shortcut between the two ends of a line, and find the point farthest from it.
If that point sits outside your tolerance, keep it, and repeat on each half.
If not, drop every point in between.
The bigger the tolerance, the fewer points survive.

scenes.title: One shape at a time
lines: Now run it on the map one county at a time.
These two neighbors share a border, but each county stores its own copy and simplifies it alone.
They keep different points, so the border splits in two.
Gold marks the gaps that belong to no county.
Red marks the land that both of them claim.

scenes.title: Broken shapes
lines: A single shape can break, too.
Drop the points on this headland, and the lake ends up outside its own island.
Straighten the far shore of this inlet, and it cuts right through the spit.
And a small islet collapses into a line with no area at all.
Each of these is an invalid geometry.

scenes.title: Topology first
lines: A topology-preserving simplifier starts from the structure instead.
Topology is which shapes touch, which borders they share, and what sits inside what.
Each shared border becomes one arc, stored once.
Where three borders meet is a node, and nodes never move.
Each arc is simplified a single time, and both neighbors use the result.
There's only one copy, so the two sides can't drift apart.

scenes.title: Checking every shortcut
lines: It also checks each shortcut before taking it.
Would the new segment cross another line? Would it sweep a lake to the wrong side?
If so, that point stays.
The lake stays on its island, the inlet stays open, and the islet keeps at least a triangle.

scenes.title: Side by side
lines: Here are both at once, with the tolerance climbing.
On the left, every border tears into slivers.
On the right, the map stays seamless.
It keeps a few more points where it has to, and stores each border only once.

scenes.title: Where to find it
lines: In PostGIS, ST_Simplify works one shape at a time and runs no checks.
ST_SimplifyPreserveTopology keeps each shape valid, but it can't see the neighbors, so shared borders can still pull apart.
For a whole map, use ST_CoverageSimplify, or an arc-based tool like mapshaper or TopoJSON.
Simplify the borders, not the shapes.
